evidence.text: To design a thin film coating using Nb2O5 and SiO2, we first implemented the transfer matrix method in MATLAB. We choose an arbitrary number of alternate layers N and initialized the thicknesses di randomly. We propagate a plane wave through the stack [air, glass, thin-film, BHJ, glass, air] and maximize the reflection at the BHJ/glass interface in the visible region (500-650 nm), and also maximize the transmission of NIR light (750-900 nm) into the BHJ. We used a regularization parameter ρ to balance between the two objectives and create a final objective function which is then fed into the MATLAB nonlinear optimization function 'optimproblem'. The optimization problem was run for several values of N, di, and ρ, with angle of incidence (θopt) set to 20°. To maintain high imaging resolution, we aimed to keep our total thickness below 1 μm and hence we settled on using a total of N = 12 total layers for our design. The resulting design was tweaked using the regularization parameter until we saw satisfactory performance across both NIR and visible wavelengths. The final thicknesses are given by: [61, 69, 69, 103, 62, 107, 60, 104, 60, 100, 62, 55] nm, where the first layer is Nb2O5, the second is SiO2, and so forth. The Y6/rubrene/DBP BHJ is positioned after the last layer in this stack. This design was provided to the thin film foundry Lohnstar Optics and was deposited on 1-mm thick 1" diameter B-270 glass substrates using DC magnetron sputtering.

evidence.title: Finding the UV–Visible Path Forward: Proceedings of the Community Workshop to Plan the Future of UV/Visible Space Astrophysics
evidence.text: Narrowband transmittance filters based on Al/MgF 2 multilayers are another classical coating, which have been used in space instrumentation. They can be designed to peak at any wavelength down to 120 nm. Their main drawback is that peak transmittance is relatively low. Reflective multilayer coatings based on two dielectrics have higher peak performance but lower out-ofband rejection than Al/MgF 2 transmittance filters. The main material combinations are (MgF 2 or AlF 3 )/(LaF 3 or GdF 3 ). Narrowband mirrors based on these materials have been obtained for a wavelength as short as 121 nm (Rodríguez de Marcos et al. 2015) and ~135-140 nm (Zukic and Torr 1992;Gatto et al. 2002). For still shorter wavelengths, a narrowband reflective coating peaked at ~100 nm based on an Al-LiF-SiC-LiF multilayer has been developed (Rodríguez-de Marcos 2013). Its band is suitable to image H Lyman β (102.6 nm) and O VI lines (103.2-103.8 nm) and to reject longer wavelengths like H Lyman α (121.6 nm).

As the angle of incidence increases, the pass band shifts towards the blue, but the large refractive index of GaP (~3.5) reduces the change in the optical path with angle by causing the rays to stay close to the normal. The DBSRs are implemented using pairs of SiO2 (108 nm)/Ta2O5 (112 nm) films, where the thicknesses are slightly different than those of a conventional DBR, as described below. SiO2 and Ta2O5 are standard thin-film optics materials, and were chosen because of their significant refractive index difference (the refractive index of SiO2 is ~1.45 and that of Ta2O5 is ~2.1 in the visible to near infrared). The large difference in the refractive index is required to achieve sufficient reflectance with minimal number of layers, as in conventional DBRs. The calculated reflectance spectra of DBSRs are shown in Figure 2a, for increasing numbers of SiO2/Ta2O5 pairs. The reflectance in the wavelength ranges of 350-400 nm and 680-950 nm increases with the number of pairs, while maintaining high visible transmittance. We would like to emphasize here that our DBSRs are different from DBRs because conventional DBRs cannot simultaneously achieve high R at the UV and near-IR ranges (350-400 nm and 680-950 nm); for example, Figure 2b shows the calculated reflectance of conventional DBRs with a target center wavelength of 780 nm, where one pair is composed of SiO2 (134 nm)/Ta2O5 (94 nm), with each thickness corresponding to λ/4n, where λ is the wavelength of 780 nm and n is the refractive index (nSiO2 = 1.45 and nTa2O5 = 2.08 at 780 nm).

evidence.title: Highly suppressed solar absorption in a daytime radiative cooler designed by genetic algorithm
evidence.text: The optimization was performed to minimize the objective function in Eq. (6). To optimize the design of up to 10 layer multilayer emitter, we used an evolutionary optimization algorithm of a GA that is inspired by natural evolution theory. As the optimization method progressed, the solution was improved through iterative operations of selection, mutation, and crossover (Figure 1A). In order to expand the design space for optimization, we optimized not only the structural parameter of thicknesses but also the material type of each layer for up to 10 layer multilayer emitter. For multilayer structures, many dielectric materials can be fabricated using thin film deposition. Among the many possible materials in nature, the following four materials were selected: SiO 2 , Si 3 N 4 , MgF 2 , and HfO 2 for their excellent chemical/thermal resistance and durability. The chosen four material candidates are then indexed for material optimization (Table 1). Through optimization, appropriate materials are recommended, and thicknesses are designed for the desired optical function. The multilayer structure to be designed consists of up to 10 layers of 1D photonic crystal on top of silver reflecting layer. We also added a layer of Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) on top, which is known to have a high transmittance in the solar region and emissivity at the atmospheric window. The middle 10 layer of 1D photonic crystals and a bottom silver layer reduce reflection in the solar region. The top PDMS is responsible for high emissivity in the atmospheric window. Overall, GA was performed to optimize the total 21 variables of the thickness of the top PDMS layer, and types of materials and thickness of each layer in the middle 10 layers (Table 2). A rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA) method was used to obtain absorption spectra. To determine appropriate weights in l, we performed five optimizations each for three different weights = 1, 5, and 10, and the optimized Q Sun and Q net are shown in Figure 1B and C. Not surprisingly, it can be seen that the solar absorption decreases with increasing weights due to the weight of the objective function, but the total optimized net cooling flux also decreases.

evidence.title: Quantum annealing for combinatorial optimization: a benchmarking study
evidence.text: Real-world problems Material optimization is selected to represent real-world problems, with the design of planar multilayers (PMLs) optical film as a testbed for benchmarking. PMLs can be seen in many applications. For example, they have been explored for transparent radiative cooling windows to address global warming by emitting thermal radiation through the atmospheric window (8 μm < λ < 13 μm) 4 , while transmitting visible photons. PMLs consist of layers with one of four dielectric materials: silicon dioxide, silicon nitride, aluminum oxide, and titanium dioxide. The configuration of these layers can be expressed as a binary vector, where each layer is assigned a two-digit binary label. Optical characteristics and corresponding figure-of-merit (FOM) of the PML can be calculated by solving Maxwell's equations using the transfer matrix method (TMM). To formulate QUBOs, layer configurations (input binary vectors) and their FOMs (outputs) are used to train the FM model. FM learns the linear and quadratic coefficients, effectively modeling the optimization landscape of the material system. QUBO matrices are then generated using these coefficients 30,31 . PML configurations are randomly generated for training datasets, and their FOMs are calculated using TMM. The resulting QUBO matrices represent real-world materials optimization problems, characterized by highly dense (fully connected) configurations (Fig. S1), which are used for the benchmarking study in Fig. 1.

method_findings.reusable_principle: Use quarter-wave optical thickness (lambda0/(4*n)) layers as building blocks for high-reflection mirrors, with modified outer layer thickness (such as double quarter-wave of low-index material or lambda0/8) to improve environmental durability and spectral performance. Layer sequence starts with high-index material on substrate and ends with low-index material.
method_findings.applicability: Suitable for high-reflection band design in HfO2/SiO2 systems on fused silica substrates where layer count is constrained (up to 30 layers). Effective for creating stopbands with well-defined center wavelengths.
method_findings.limitations: Quarter-wave designs produce comparatively narrow high-transmittance and high-reflection bands. Outer layer modifications require independent verification for specific wavelength bands. Does not inherently address dual-band filtering without additional cavity structures.

method_findings.method_name: Genetic algorithm for multilayer parameter optimization
method_findings.reusable_principle: Apply evolutionary optimization with selection, mutation, and crossover operations to optimize both layer thicknesses and material types simultaneously. Index material candidates for optimization and expand design space beyond fixed material assignments. Iteratively improve solutions through generations while respecting layer count constraints.
method_findings.applicability: Appropriate when optimizing multilayer structures with bounded variables (layer thicknesses, layer sequence, number of layers up to 30). Useful for dual-band filtering objectives where analytical design is difficult.
method_findings.limitations: Requires objective function formulation specific to the application. Computational cost increases with layer count. Material candidate selection must be pre-defined based on fabrication constraints. Convergence to global optimum is not guaranteed.

method_findings.reusable_principle: Replace metallic reflecting layers with all-dielectric multilayer mirrors forming a Fabry-Perot interferometer structure. Use dielectric mirrors (9 or more layers each) separated by a resonance cavity layer with optical thickness of half-wavelength. Multiple cavities can be coupled in series to modify pass band shape from triangular to smoother profiles.
method_findings.applicability: Suitable for narrow bandpass filtering in specific wavelength bands (such as 1530-1565 nm for QKD). Effective when high transmittance in pass band and high reflectance in stop bands are required.
method_findings.limitations: Layer count can exceed 30 for high-performance designs (mirrors typically require 9+ layers each). Pass band shape is initially triangular and requires coupling for smoothing. Cavity thickness must be precisely controlled for resonance condition.

method_findings.reusable_principle: Incorporate interlayers between discontinuous high-low index interfaces to create graded refractive index profiles. Vary intermediate layer composition through distinct cycle ratios of high and low index materials (such as HfO2 and SiO2). This reduces interface discontinuities compared to conventional multilayer stacks.
method_findings.applicability: Applicable to HfO2/SiO2 systems on fused silica substrates. Useful for antireflection coatings and reducing scattering losses at interfaces. Compatible with layer count constraints.
method_findings.limitations: Requires fabrication capability for composition-graded layers. Refractive index of intermediate layers varies with composition cycle ratio and must be characterized. Total thickness optimization may differ from conventional quarter-wave designs.

method_findings.method_name: Needle optimization technique for non-quarter-wave designs
method_findings.reusable_principle: Use needle optimization technique incorporated into thin-film design software to optimize non-quarter-wave optical thickness designs for multiple wavelength targets simultaneously. Define performance targets for each working wavelength with minimum band width specifications. Include environmental durability constraints such as outermost layer material and minimum thickness.
method_findings.applicability: Appropriate for multi-wavelength high-reflection coatings (such as 3-wavelength HR at 632.8, 810, and 1550 nm). Suitable when quarter-wave designs cannot meet all wavelength targets simultaneously.
method_findings.limitations: Requires specialized optimization software. Layer count can become large (38 layers demonstrated) which may exceed 30-layer constraint. Non-quarter-wave designs present fabrication challenges for thickness control. Outermost layer constraints must be incorporated into optimization.

method_findings.method_name: Antireflection coating for coupled cavity structures
method_findings.reusable_principle: Add antireflection coatings to reduce reflectance oscillations in pass bands of coupled cavity structures. AR coating thickness equals half the dielectric spacer thickness and uses the same material. This doubles overall transmittance and smooths oscillations associated with coupled cavity modes, reducing reflectance variation in pass band.
method_findings.applicability: Useful for improving transmittance in bandpass filter designs with Fabry-Perot or coupled cavity structures. Applicable when pass band reflectance oscillations need suppression.
method_findings.limitations: AR coating design is specific to single cavity and may require adjustment for multi-cavity systems. Adds additional layers to total count. Effectiveness depends on accurate spacer thickness knowledge.

strategy_plan.planning_summary: This portfolio tests three distinct strategy axes for a dual-band filter: (1) a periodic Bragg stack centered on the visible stopband, (2) a chirped thickness-modulated stack to broaden visible rejection, and (3) a defect-cavity stack to sharpen telecom transmission. These axes are genuinely different because they rely on different physical mechanisms - Bragg interference versus graded index versus cavity resonance - and can succeed or fail independently. The 30-layer constraint is respected in all routes. Literature L02, L18, L34 support periodic and optimization approaches; L04 supports thickness modulation; L03, L15, L33 address HfO2/SiO2 coating durability relevant to space applications. No route optimizes refractive index; all tune geometry only.
